newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK investors pop corks as handover nears.
newsitem.headline: HK investors pop corks as handover nears.

text.p: After a decade spent fretting about Hong Kong's return to China, stock investors are now celebrating.
With just days to go before the handover, much of the uncertainty -- including fears of social unrest in China after the death of Deng Xiaoping -- has been removed.

Some even welcome closer integration between Hong Kong and China as a business opportunity. And not even plans by the future Hong Kong government to dilute civil liberties have shaken their faith in a more prosperous future.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index has soared by 14 percent since the start of the year, after adding 34 percent in 1996, and hit a record high of 15,322.33 points last Monday.
It surged 174.06 points, or 1.17 percent, on Wednesday to close at 15,065.02.
"A political re-rating began last August due to a rise in confidence in Hong Kong," said Frederick Tsang, head of research at BNP PrimeEast Securities.
"There will be a further re-rating due to the economic integration between Hong Kong and China."
Tsang sees the index heading to 18,500 a year from now. "Investors are giving the future government the benefit of the doubt."
Squabbles between Britain and China after their December 1984 agreement on the return of Hong Kong unnerved the market.

"One thing that unsettles stock markets is uncertainty and no man can serve two masters," said Robert Rountree, regional strategist at Nomura Research Institute. "So if you have got two masters, you are going to have a lot of uncertainty."
"With Hong Kong now going back to China, it has removed a tremendous amount of uncertainty. Even if you may not like the policy, you know that you are only dealing with one body."
The reappointment in February of Hong Kong's top officials to serve in future leader Tung Chee-hwa's post-colonial administration was a boost for confidence.

"There has been an understanding that the laissez-faire principles inherent in Hong Kong is an area that China has agreed not to interfere with," said Andrew Fernow, head of research at Vickers Ballas.
"While it has interfered with the process of political reform, it certainly has not tried to change the economic policies which make Hong Kong successful."

Hong Kong's democratically elected legislature will be dissolved immediately after the handover and replaced with a body handpicked by China. New laws aimed at pro-democracy activists will restrict the right to demonstrate.
Fernow noted that the death in February of China's paramount leader Deng had failed to spark the internal conflict within the Chinese government that some had feared.
"Investors weigh the potential rewards against the risks and conclude that China is still an opportunity for business."
In fact, closer ties with China's expanding economy have some analysts calling for a further re-rating of the Hong Kong market as it takes on the features of an emerging economy.
"We are not dealing with Hong Kong, we are dealing with China and this could be another phase of the bull run for China/Hong Kong," said Yamaichi International head of reserch Alex Tang.
But Nikko Research Center chief strategist Marshall Mays said investors had just moved from extreme pessimism to extreme optimism and current prices suggested "unjustified optimism".
"One should be optimistic about the commercial success of Hong Kong but whether it justifies multiples of 15 to 17 times earnings is a big difference," he said.
However, Rountree said a re-rating had yet to be completed and the index could reach 19,000 points by the end of next year.
"I don't think that the political risk premium has been priced out. At the moment there is not the money," he said.

Once Hong Kong's new government announced its policy to deal with rising property prices and the earnings cycle became clearer, quality investors would join the rally, he said. "When it eventually comes, it could be a beauty."
